statements.quote: In AI, we don't always know the right answer immediately.
Instead, we use a **Loss Function** — a scoreboard that measures how wrong the AI's predictions are.
The goal is to make the loss as small as possible; zero is not always attainable, because noisy data leave an irreducible error.
To do that, the AI has to figure out which direction to move to find the bottom of the valley.
Imagine you are standing on a foggy mountain.
You can't see the bottom, but you can feel the ground under your feet.
To find the way down, you:
**Look Ahead:** Take a tiny “probe” step ($h$) to the side.
**Check the Change:** See if that step made your height go up or down.
**Calculate the Slope:** This tells you how steep the hill is right where you are standing.
In math, we write this simple “steepness check” like this:
Long before anybody wrote $f'(x)$, Greek geometers were already comparing a curve with a straight line.

statements.quote: **The “probe” step:** The orange secant is what the AI actually measures: it compares $f(x)$ with $f(x+h)$.
With a big $h$ it averages the steepness over a wide stretch and misses the true slope (the green tangent).
Drag the look-ahead slider to the left and watch the error shrink until the two lines coincide — that limit is the derivative.

**Learning in action:** Click **“Take one step”** or **“Run descent.”** Each update moves $x$ by $-\eta \cdot \text{slope}$, so the ball takes big steps where the ground is steep and tiny ones near the bottom.
**The learning rate matters:** On the valley $x^2$, push $\eta$ above $0.5$: the ball starts to zig-zag across the bottom.
Above $1.0$ every step overshoots by more than it gains and the ball flies off — the same instability that makes real training runs “diverge.”
**Getting stuck:** Try **“Two valleys.”** Starting on the right, descent settles in the shallow valley and stops, because the slope there is zero — even though the valley on the left is deeper.
The ball only feels the ground under its feet.
This is the situation every learning algorithm is in: it cannot see the whole landscape, only the height and the slope where it stands.
Find the lowest point with eight probes — then compare yourself with gradient descent, which gets exactly the same information.

1350–1425) and his successors obtained infinite series for $\pi$, sine and cosine around 1400, more than two centuries before Europe rediscovered them \cite{madhava_mactutor}.

Their work was not a formal derivative, but it handled change and accumulation with infinite processes long before Newton and Leibniz made such processes a general method.
Above, we looked at a function with only one input ($x$).
For that, we use the standard $d$ to represent a derivative.
However, AI models usually have millions of inputs.
When we deal with multiple variables, we use the **partial derivative** symbol: $\partial$.

The symbol $\partial$ for partial derivatives appears in one of its first known uses in the work of the Marquis de Condorcet in \citeyear{condorcet1770}; the modern partial-derivative notation $\partial f/\partial x$ was created by \citeauthor{legendre1786} in \citetitle{legendre1786} (\citeyear{legendre1786}) — a suggestion he later abandoned — and was only popularized after Jacobi reintroduced it in 1841 (according to \citeauthor{historyofmathematicalnotation}, Vol.
Calculus became a general method in the seventeenth century.

Newton called the quantities he differentiated *fluents* and their rates *fluxions*; his *Method of Fluxions* circulated in manuscript long before it appeared in print in 1736 \cite{newton1736fluxions}.

Leibniz, working independently, chose the differential notation $dy/dx$ and the long $\int$; his *Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis* (1684) announced the algorithm to a wider public \cite{leibniz1684nova}.
Their priority dispute was bitter, but the notation that survived is largely Leibniz's.
The modern definition is a limit, and that is a nineteenth-century achievement.
Cauchy treated the derivative as the limit of the difference quotient in his 1823 *Résumé des leçons sur le calcul infinitésimal* \cite{cauchy1823resume}.

Weierstrass went further, replacing talk of infinitely small quantities with the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ inequalities that make “arbitrarily close” precise; his 1872 example of a continuous curve with no derivative anywhere showed why the rigor was needed \cite{weierstrass_mactutor}.
The secant in the lab is an approximation; the derivative is what those secants approach.
The partial derivative is a way to measure how a single variable affects the final result while ignoring everything else.
* **The Problem:** In a complex system, changing two things at once makes it impossible to know which change caused the result.
* **The Solution:** We “freeze” all variables except one.
We treat those frozen variables as if they were plain, unmoving numbers (constants).
* **The Symbol:** We write $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ to say: “Find the slope of function $f$, but only look at the $x$ direction.”
Imagine an AI trying to predict house prices.

statements.quote: At the current point $(x, y) = (4, 1)$, the AI combines these individual slopes into a **Gradient Vector**:
This vector gives the local direction and rate of steepest increase; the AI moves against it by a step set by the learning rate.
Just like the **“Take 1 Step Down”** button, the AI uses these numbers to move toward the minimum error by updating each variable independently:
A gradient is more than a list of partials: it is the direction in which the function rises fastest, and its length is that maximal rate of change.
The same idea gives the **directional derivative** in any unit direction $u$, namely $\nabla f \cdot u$.

In one dimension the only directions are left and right, which is why a single slope suffices; with millions of weights, the gradient is the compact first-order summary of “which way is uphill” that the model can afford \cite{hadamard1908}.
* $x_\text{new} = x_\text{old} - (\text{Learning Rate} \times 8)$
* $y_\text{new} = y_\text{old} - (\text{Learning Rate} \times 6)$
You've learned how to find the slope of one hill.
But a Deep AI is like a **chain of hills**.
When the AI makes a mistake at the very end (the output), it has to figure out which “knob” at the very beginning (the input) caused it.
This is called **Backpropagation**, and it relies on the **Chain Rule**.
Imagine three gears connected in a line: Gear A, Gear B, and Gear C.
* If you turn Gear A, it turns Gear B.
* If Gear B turns, it turns Gear C.
If you want to know how fast Gear C moves when you touch Gear A, you just multiply the ratios:
In AI, we calculate the error at the end first.
We then pass that “error message” backward through the chain.
Each layer multiplies the incoming message by its own local slope.
